> with low latency

Audio format latency is generally determined by the duration of a decodable block. If you're recording in real time for VoIP, that duration is the time it will take for the block to be done for others to listen.

But since the context here is pre-encoded audio files, latency means pretty much nothing.

> But since the context here is pre-encoded audio files, latency means pretty much nothing.

True, since this PR doesn't add the ability to decode raw Opus streams, although I wonder if you could make that possible.

I did however benchmark the `seek()` operation, and it's over 10x faster for Opus:

Seeking to 125.3s in a 728s file:
- OGG Vorbis: `0.002816 seconds` -> 5x per frame at 60FPS.
- OGG Opus: `0.000322 seconds` -> 52x per frame at 60FPS.

<details>
<summary>See benchmark code</summary>

```gdscript
func benchmark(asp: AudioStreamPlayer, use_opus: bool) -> void:
	asp.stop()
	if use_opus:
		asp.stream = symphony_no_6_opus
	else:
		asp.stream = symphony_no_6_vorbis
	asp.play()
	
	var start_usec: int = Time.get_ticks_usec()
	asp.seek(125.3)
	var end_usec: int = Time.get_ticks_usec()
	print("Opus" if use_opus else "Vorbis", ": ", (end_usec - start_usec) / 1_000_000.0, " seconds")
```
</details>

Quick binary size comparison on a stripped Linux x86_64 release template (`production=yes lto=full`):

- `master`: 75,755,856 bytes
- This PR: 76,069,472 bytes (+314 KB)

The size increase is significant, but keep in mind it lets you ship smaller audio files with the same quality as before. With most game soundtracks weighing at least 50 MB, you'll likely save at least 5 MB in the soundtrack alone, which results in the total game size decreasing. That's not counting situations where you use compressed audio for ambient sounds, voice clips and so on. This can also greatly reduce the size of update/DLC PCKs and delta patches (since these are compressed files, delta compression isn't effective in the first place).

The main downside would be that non-game applications will be larger, but in general, these benefit a lot from using custom builds as they can disable a lot of features and lose no functionality whatsoever.

For a web release export template (WASM file size), the increase is less significant:

- `master`: 38,182,757 bytes
- This PR: 38,306,912 bytes (+124 KB)

We could choose not to support Opus as streams on the web platform if we wanted to avoid any size increase whatsoever, and constrain it to sample-based playback. However, as I understand it, this is not ideal for playing soundtracks. It would also lead to a discrepancy in support across platforms, which can result in surprises when exporting. cc @adamscott

> MP3 - released 34 years ago, very outdated compression, and [can't be looped seamlessly due to padding](https://sound.stackexchange.com/questions/25846/is-it-possible-to-loop-mp3-without-gaps).

The loop gap is usually caused by the MP3 file having LAME tags. Note that the built-in MP3 decoder (dr_mp3) has support for parsing and skipping them.

Now that you mention it, architecture-specific source files are supposed be compiled for their respective architectures. And this is where a problem comes in:

- Every source in `x86` folders should be compiled for x86 and x86_64 systems.
- Every source in the `arm` folder should be compiled for ARM systems. This is a little complicated as the build system expects you to run `arm2gnu.pl` over `.s` files in a specific way.

They're pretty much optional, but desired for performance.

> I'm not sure about the semantics of containers like `TightLocalVector`, is it necessary to use it here?

It is desired to avoid manual allocations/deallocations as much as possible in the codebase.

It's pretty much these steps:
1. Convert `data` from a `void` pointer to `TightLocalVector<uint8_t>`.
2. In `AudioStreamOpus::set_data()` you hand over `p_data` to `data` instead of allocating.
3. `AudioStreamOpus::clear_data()` should just call `clear()` on `data` instead of deallocating.
4. When you want the actual pointer, you just call `data.ptr()`.
5. No need for `AudioStreamOpus::~AudioStreamOpus()`. The data will be cleared anyway as the vector will be deleted.

Once again, `AudioStreamMP3` can be a nice reference.

I can confirm your error does happen when a sound finishes playing. The line the error refers to is `ERR_FAIL_COND_V(!active, 0);` inside `_mix_internal`, which implies that `_mix_internal` is being called while `active` is false.
The other audio stream implementations (MP3 and Vorbis) simply return 0 if `active` is false, instead of printing an error. So, I changed it to do that as well, and it works. Can you check it works for you as well?

I think that Opus should be in the engine, because any game that uses music, sound effects or voice lines can save a large amount of data by compressing as Opus.

If you would like to minimize the engine's footprint, surely it would make more sense to remove MP3? MP3 is pretty much a direct downgrade to every other encoding.

If it's a GDExtension, no one is going to use it, and its compatibility will be dubious. Since many GDExtensions don't work on certain platforms, I wouldn't want to risk my game not working on a platform like Android, just so I could use the Opus encoding.

Also, on an unrelated note, may I ask which parts of your addon were written with AI? As @novadragonDOTspace pointed out, you said this:
> This is ideal work for an AI because it's not a creative project since there is basically only one way to combine the components of opus, libopus and ogg.

Have you personally verified the security of the code?

For what it's worth, a GDExtension that adds Opus support will be larger in file size than built-in Opus support. This is because it also statically links against godot-cpp and can't reuse the engine's own libogg library.

The Linux release `.so` for https://github.com/goatchurchprime/godot-ogg-opus/releases/latest is 945 KB (400 KB compressed), much more than the 233 KB increase (130 KB compressed) from this PR. This means you'd need significantly more audio to convert to Opus to reach the "inflection point" where Opus support actually decreases your project's file size (which is arguably the end goal of this PR).

There might be a way to reduce this size somewhat (is the extension compiled with LTO?), but it'll always be larger than a built-in implementation. Even with LTO enabled, LTO won't be able to be as aggressive in a small library compared to a single large statically-linked binary.

I assume the added size might not be a huge deal, since this is a module: it should be trivial to recompile the engine with or without it, if I'm not wrong.

Also, if Ogg Opus is superior than Vorbis in every way, maybe Vorbis can be deprecated if this PR is merged.

The AI policy doesn't apply to addons.  Godot has a very sophisticated addon system where the extensions bind seamlessly into the editor, and this is the ideal place to work on features and put them into use without having to wait years and multiple releases for their merits to be recognized by the maintainers.

A working addon that has proved itself can be migrated into the core engine, as happened with the Jolt physics engine, which was widely used as a plugin at first.

If anyone makes a better non-AI opus playing plugin and puts it in the asset store, I'll happily delete mine in its favour.

Tested this PR (backported to 4.7.2) and re-checked the code at 82388ab. Four issues in `modules/opus/audio_stream_opus.cpp`:

1. **Use after free when `data` changes during playback.** `instantiate_playback()` passes `data.ptr()` to `op_open_memory()` (L188), which keeps the raw pointer. A later `set_data()` with larger data (L233) reallocates the vector, so the playback's decoder reads freed memory. With data of the same or smaller size, the bytes are overwritten in place under the decoder. A fix: store `data` as a `Vector<uint8_t>` and give each playback its own copy (copy on write, so no extra allocation). Relatedly, `seek()` clamps with the stream's current `get_length()` (L139) rather than the playback's own `op_pcm_total()`.
2. **`bpm` and `beat_count` do not affect looping.** With `loop` on and a positive `bpm` and `beat_count`, `AudioStreamOggVorbis` and `AudioStreamMP3` restart at `beat_count * 60 / bpm` seconds with a short crossfade (`FADE_SIZE`). `AudioStreamOpus` only stores the values (L287 to 305) and loops at the end of the file. Example: a 3 s file with `bpm = 120` and `beat_count = 2` should loop after 1 s. When this is added, compute the endpoint in `int64_t` (`beat_count * 48000 * 60` overflows `int` at 746 beats), and reset the loop fade state in `start()` as `AudioStreamPlaybackOggVorbis::start()` does, since `AudioStreamInteractive` reuses playbacks.
3. **A non-looping stream reports a full block at the end.** At end of file, `_mix_internal()` zero-fills, sets `todo = 0` (L72 to 76) and returns `p_frames - todo`, that is `p_frames` (L81). `AudioStreamPlaybackResampled` then treats the silent tail as audio. A voice line with 53,011 decoded frames reports 53,120, which delays completion. Returning the number of frames actually decoded (as Vorbis does) fixes it. This may also be behind the `Condition "!active"` error reported above.
4. **`OP_HOLE` ends playback.** `op_read_float_stereo()` returns `OP_HOLE` for a recoverable gap, such as a missing page. `_mix_internal()` treats any negative value as fatal (L54 to 60), so `AudioServer` drops the playback as ended. Removing one middle page from a 20 s file ends playback near 7 s. Continuing to decode on `OP_HOLE` fixes it.

Since the WebM pull request is now working, I decided to take the time to enable the Opus SIMD optimizations to reduce the CPU usage from the audio side, and they seem to be working correctly.

| Architecture | Optimizations |
| --- | --- |
| `Windows x64`, `Linux x64`, `Android x64` | `SSE`, `SSE2`, `SSE4.1` |
| `Windows x32`, `Linux x32`, `Android x32` | `SSE`, `SSE2` |
| `Linux ARM64`, `Android ARM64` | `NEON` |
| `Windows ARM64`, `Linux ARM32`, `Android ARM32`, `Web WASM32` | (None) |

There's more detailed info about it on the [OpusGdextension](https://github.com/Joy-less/OpusGdextension) page. In particular, I used the x86 optimizations that [Godot already requires](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/about/system_requirements.html), and the NEON optimizations that are guaranteed on ARM64, and removed the legacy ARM optimizations that aren't relevant anymore. I couldn't add the NEON optimizations on Windows ARM64, because Godot is using `setup-mingw` which doesn't provide `arm_neon.h` for ARM64.

I've tested the optimizations on Windows x64 and Android ARM64, but if the other builds cause issues, they can be disabled simply by commenting out the if-branches under `# Add architecture-specific optimizations`.

While I was working on it, I checked the size difference. For `OpusGdextension.windows.template_debug.x86_64.dll`, the uncompressed size decreased from 775,680 bytes to 773,120 bytes. So it looks like the optimizations can actually slightly reduce the binary size.
